blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The High Court is the highest judicial authority at the State level, governed by Articles 214 to 231 in Part VI of the Constitution.
High Court judges are appointed by the President and hold office until attaining the age of 62 years.
Under Article 226, High Courts possess writ jurisdiction for protecting Fundamental Rights and other legal rights, making its scope wider than the Supreme Court's writ power.
High Courts act as Courts of Record under Article 215, meaning their judgments are preserved permanently and they hold the power to punish for contempt.
Prohibition is issued before a lower court decision to stop proceedings, whereas Certiorari is issued after a decision to quash an illegal order.

blocks.content: The High Court is the highest judicial authority at the State level.
It occupies an extremely important position in the Indian judicial system as it protects the Constitution, safeguards Fundamental Rights, and ensures justice within the State.
The provisions relating to the High Court are given in Part VI of the Indian Constitution (Articles 214 to 231).
Every State in India has a High Court, though some High Courts have jurisdiction over more than one State or Union Territory.

blocks.content: The number of judges is decided by the President depending on workload and population. The Chief Justice of the High Court is appointed by the President in consultation with:

items:
• Chief Justice of India
  • Governor of the State

blocks.content: Judges of the High Court are appointed by the President of India. Consultation is done with:

items:
• Chief Justice of India
  • Governor of the State
  • Chief Justice of the High Court (for other judges) This ensures independence of judiciary.
Chief Justice of the High Court (for other judges) This ensures independence of judiciary.

blocks.content: A person must satisfy the following conditions:

items:
• Must be a citizen of India
  • Must have held a judicial office for at least 10 years OR
  • Must have been an advocate of a High Court for at least 10 years
Must be a citizen of India
Must have held a judicial office for at least 10 years OR
Must have been an advocate of a High Court for at least 10 years
• Judge holds office till the age of 62 years
Judge holds office till the age of 62 years

• Same procedure as Supreme Court judges
  • By impeachment
  • Proven misbehavior or incapacity
  • Special majority in Parliament
Same procedure as Supreme Court judges

• Salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State
  • Cannot be reduced after appointment
  • Ensures independence of judiciary
Salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State

Original jurisdiction means cases which can be directly heard by the High Court. Includes:

items:

  • Election petitions
  • Matters related to enforcement of Fundamental Rights
Matters related to enforcement of Fundamental Rights

blocks.content: Fundamental Rights give rights to citizens.
Writs provide remedies for violation of those rights. Thus, writs are the soul of Fundamental Rights.
Through writs, High Courts exercise judicial review. They

items:
• Laws are constitutional
  • Authorities act legally
  • Justice is delivered

blocks.content: High Court exercises control over all subordinate courts within its jurisdiction. It can:

items:
• Call for records
  • Issue guidelines
  • Ensure proper functioning of lower courts
Ensure proper functioning of lower courts

blocks.content: High Court has administrative control over:

items:
• Appointment of district judges
  • Promotion and transfer of judges
  • Disciplinary action

blocks.content: High Court is a Court of Record. This means:

items:
• Its judgments are preserved permanently
  • It can punish for contempt of court
It can punish for contempt of court
Article 226 writ power of High Court is wider than Supreme Court's Article 32 power because it covers legal rights in addition to Fundamental Rights.
Salaries and allowances of High Court judges are charged directly on the Consolidated Fund of the State.
Mandamus cannot be issued against the President, State Governors, or private individuals.
Difference between Prohibition and Certiorari: Prohibition is invoked before the decision (prevents action), while Certiorari is invoked after the decision (quashes order).

RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN HIGH COURT AND SUPREME COURT

items:
• High Court is subordinate to Supreme Court
  • Appeals lie to Supreme Court
  • Supreme Court can transfer cases
  • Supreme Court judgments are binding
High Court is subordinate to Supreme Court

• Protector of Fundamental Rights
  • Guardian of Constitution at State level
  • Controls subordinate judiciary
  • Ensures rule of law
Guardian of Constitution at State level

• Heavy pendency of cases
  • Shortage of judges
  • Delay in justice
  • Workload pressure

blocks.content: The High Court is a pillar of the Indian judicial system.
It ensures justice, protects constitutional rights, and maintains balance between State power and individual liberty.
Its role is vital in upholding democracy and rule of law in India.
